The hint

Decided 2026-11-11. Tooltip had 0 call sites: its only two users had become IconButtons, which showed a native title, and rule/tooltip-one-hint forbids both together. The choice was to retire the component or to make it the hint IconButton shows. It is the hint, for these reasons:

  • A native title never shows on keyboard focus, so a keyboard user of a tool strip of 25 glyphs

had no way to read what a key does short of a screen reader. The layer's box shows at once on focus.

  • The native box is the platform's: its own delay, its own face, in neither theme. One styled hint

everywhere is the measured Cursor box the layer already carried and nothing drew.

  • It costs the call sites nothing: IconButton already took the string as title.

How it is built, and why:

  • One box on <body>, in the viewport's coordinates, not a child of each control: the tool

strip, the sidebar and the assistant's panes clip their overflow, and a box inside them would be cut at the pane's edge. It also keeps IconButton a single <button>, so no surface's layout or selector changes.

  • Placed by script: below the control (where the platform's hint fell, clear of the menu bar

above the tool strip), above it when there is no room below, and slid along the window's edge rather than across it. placement on the wrapper only names the preferred side; the align prop is gone, because the hold inside the window does its job without the caller knowing where the control sits.

  • Timing: 0.4s under a resting mouse or pen; at once when another hint went away within 0.3s,

so sweeping the strip reads every key; at once on keyboard focus (focus a key moved, so a click's focus does not raise it; the second pass below replaced the first pass's :focus-visible test); never under a finger, which has no hover.

  • Dismissal: Escape, a press, a click, typing, a scroll, a resize and the window losing focus put it

away, and it stays away until the pointer or the focus moves to another control. Escape is not consumed: a menu that closes on Escape still closes.

  • Hidden from assistive tech (aria-hidden): the box repeats the aria-label, and a second

announcement of the same words is noise. It is not a role="tooltip" description.

  • The name stays on aria-label, and no native title is rendered, so the two hints cannot

stack.

One hint in the whole layer (2026-11-11, second pass)

Button, Chip, Tab and Field moved onto the box with no call-site change: each still takes title, and none renders the native attribute. What moved with them:

  • The name and the description, per component. The hint is the name only where there is no

other (IconButton: aria-label). A Button, a Chip or a Tab has a visible label and a Field has ariaLabel, so there the hint is supplementary and is exposed as the control's description. It must be exposed somehow: the box is aria-hidden, and with the native title gone a screen reader would otherwise lose the words (the reason Save is disabled, what a tab switches to). A static Chip is a <span> with no role, where a description is not announced; its hint is for the eye only and its spec says to put nothing essential there.

  • aria-describedby, not aria-description. aria-description is one attribute and no

machinery, but it is an ARIA 1.3 working-draft attribute, and the desktop app runs in whatever system webview the machine has (WebKit on macOS, WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux), which is not evergreen everywhere. aria-describedby pointing at text is supported by every engine and screen reader pairing. The text lives in one hidden element on <body> (.ui-hint-descriptions, one <span> per control, removed with it), not beside the control: a hidden child would enter textContent and a hidden sibling would change every surface's :first-child, + and flex-gap arithmetic. A hidden element referenced by aria-describedby is still read as the description. describeByHint in src/ui/Tooltip.tsx is the one place that does this, and a surface's own element can call it.

  • A repeat is nothing. A hint equal to the label the control shows (trimmed, white space

collapsed) with no shortcut and no second line draws no box and adds no description: the chat tabs pass their title as both, and "hello, tab, hello" helps nobody.

  • A clipped label is always reachable. When a control's own box cuts its label (scrollWidth

past clientWidth), the hint's first line is the full label, whether or not the caller passed title, and what title adds drops to a second line. Tab and Chip always carry data-hint (empty when there is no title) so this works without the caller thinking of it. Assistive tech never needed it: the full text is in the element, and the ellipsis is paint.

  • The shortcut is a key cap. The explicit form is the one to write: shortcut on IconButton

and Button, data-hint-keys on any other element; it also sets aria-keyshortcuts. The old form, a title ending "(Ctrl+Z)", is still split off by IconButton and Button so the 9 existing call sites draw the cap today; there the accessible name keeps the bracket (changing a name is a behaviour change the call site should make on purpose), and no aria-keyshortcuts is added, which would say the shortcut twice. Only a bracket that is a key combination is split ("Attach a picture (or paste, or drop one)" stays text), and the attribute form never parses: a chat titled "Option (B)" must not grow a key cap.

  • 32ch, wrapped. The box was one nowrap line clipped with an ellipsis at the window's width;

a reason a control is disabled is a sentence and was cut. It now wraps at a 32ch measure, and is never wider or taller than the window less the gap on each side.

  • Focus a key moved, only. :focus-visible is true for a field on any focus and for a button a

closing dialog hands focus back to, and neither is a person asking what the control is. The hint shows on focus only when the last key pressed was one that moves focus (Tab, the arrows, Home, End, Page Up, Page Down, F6) and no press has followed it. Whichever of the pointer and the focus moved last names the control: a pointer left resting on one key no longer silences the hint of the key the keyboard moves to.

  • Not over a popup. A control whose own menu or dialog is open (aria-haspopup with

aria-expanded="true") shows no hint, and while focus is inside a menu or a dialog only that popup's own controls do. A fold key is aria-expanded too and keeps its hint: its region is in the page's flow and covers nothing. A control inside a modal <dialog> gets the box as a child of that dialog, because the top layer covers <body>.

  • Row, the last native title (2026-11-11, third pass). Row rendered the platform's

title in both forms; it now carries data-hint and ties its title as the description, with no call-site change. Three things came with it. A component with no title carries data-hint empty so its clipped label can show, and the layers panel wraps such a Row in a Tooltip: an empty host now gives way to a host around it that has words. A row's label sits beside trailing text (a shortcut, a path), so the full label a clipped control shows is the part that is cut, not the whole row run together; and a part hidden from assistive tech is skipped, because the layer's name is drawn in two pieces for the eye beside its whole text. A field's label is its value (never a password's), which is what lets Field replace the palette's hintWhenClipped.

  • Not over a select's list. A select's list opens where the box sits. A press already put the

box away; so does every key in a <select> now, except Tab and a bare modifier (Space, Enter and the arrows open the list or change the value).

  • Outside the layer. The delegation never looked at who rendered the element, so

data-hint, data-hint-keys, data-hint-note and data-hint-placement work on any element. About ninety native titles remain in the surfaces' own markup (the status toggles, the layer keys, the properties' clipped values); tooltip.md ("Adopting the hint outside the layer") is the procedure, including what happens to the accessible name each of them was getting from title.

Disabled controls

Decided 2026-11-11. A disabled Button or IconButton is aria-disabled="true" and never carries the native disabled attribute; the component refuses the click.

  • Why. A control that is blocked by something the user can fix should be able to say what

(the setup sheet's Save: "To save, choose a provider or type a base URL."). The native attribute takes the button out of the Tab order, so a keyboard user can never reach the words, and in some engines it also swallows pointer events on the button, so a mouse user cannot either; the desktop app runs in three different system webviews and the layer cannot pick the well-behaved one.

  • How the click is refused. refuseWhenDisabled (src/ui/Button.tsx, used by both) listens on

the button itself and, while aria-disabled="true", calls preventDefault and stopImmediatePropagation. That is before the caller's onClick, before any ancestor's handler (a native disabled button's click reaches nobody, and a row that selects on click must not start hearing its disabled key), and before a form takes a submit button's click. Enter and Space on a button arrive as the same click, so one guard covers the pointer and both keys.

  • What it costs. A disabled button is now a Tab stop. That is the point where it has a reason

to give, and one extra stop where it has none (the ARIA Authoring Practices guide allows keeping a disabled control focusable where a user must be able to find it). It takes the focus ring, no hover fill and no pressed fill. :disabled no longer matches these two components: a surface that styles one writes [aria-disabled="true"] (src/ui/recipe.test.ts holds the layer to it).

  • Scope. Field keeps the native disabled (a field one cannot type in should not take the

caret), and Row keeps it too (a disabled row in a menu or the palette is skipped by the list's own arrow-key handling, and nothing asks a row to explain itself yet).

A setting switched in place

Decided 2026-11-11, with Toggle. The last hand-drawn controls in the shell were the layer list's three state keys per row and the status bar's eleven drafting toggles: four raw <button aria-pressed> call sites in two files, two recipes.

  • Why not IconButton selected. It was tried and does not fit, for four reasons. Its title

is both the name and the hint, and a state key needs a name that never changes ("Outline frozen", with aria-pressed carrying the state) and a different hint (the action, "Thaw"). selected paints the .14 fill, and "on" is pressed on nearly every row, so every row would gain a fill. The state inks (off, frozen, locked, each with a light-theme step) have no prop. And its box is a circle, where the key is a 20 by 22 cell as tall as the row.

  • The state is the face's alone. No fill at rest, on or off. A glyph toggle swaps its glyph

(icon, iconOn) and takes the tone's ink; a text toggle takes the full ink and a hairline rule in --toggle-on under the word. Neither is colour alone. The fills are the layer's own: .08 under the pointer and .14 while held, which the layer keys did not have before.

  • tone is a closed set of four, mapped to tokens the app already had. neutral: off

--text-faint, on --text. absent: on --icon, off --icon-layer-off stepped 15% to the ink (light: --text-dim). info: on --icon-layer-frozen (light: --text-accent). caution: on --icon-locked (light: --warn stepped 20% to the ink). The light steps are in src/ui/ui.css under :root[data-theme="light"], the layer's first theme selector: the two mixes are not single token values, and a token per tone and state would have been six new tokens for one component. No colour was added.

  • The hint is for the eye and is not the description. Every other component exposes its hint

to assistive tech, as the name or the description, because the hint box is aria-hidden. A toggle's hint is the action a press takes now, which the name and aria-pressed already say: "Outline frozen, pressed, Thaw" says the state twice. What a screen reader must also hear (why the toggle is blocked) goes in description, as on IconButton.

  • One Tab stop is the container's. The status bar and the tool strip rove from the container

through a ref (rovingBand, src/components/ToolStrip.tsx), which sets tabIndex on each element. Toggle takes tabIndex as a prop for a container that roves through props, and writes no attribute when the prop is unset, so the two never fight.

  • A small word is as tall as its line. The status bar's line is its row less its top

hairline, and it grows under a finger; a component cannot know either. The container sets --ui-toggle-line, and the word falls back to the row height. It is the one custom property a caller sets for a layer component, and it sets a size the component cannot measure, never a look.

  • Under a finger. The small glyph keeps its 20 by 22 cell and takes the rest of 24 by 24 as an

overhang; the layer list keeps its three keys 4px apart there so the targets do not overlap (they stood flush, with 20 by 22 targets). The word is at least 24 by 24.

  • Disabled. As Button and IconButton: aria-disabled, focusable, the click refused, the face

at the disabled ink in every tone. No call site disables a toggle yet.

  • The curve. The hand-drawn keys eased on the shell's button rule (--ease-out); a Toggle

eases on the layer's measured --ease-standard, as every other component. Same 0.1s.

What stays local in a layer row

Looked at with Toggle, 2026-11-11: the row's colour swatch and its "has objects" mark, both role="img" spans drawn by src/styles.css.

  • The swatch stays local. A Swatch needs a second use, and the candidate was the properties

palette's Color row, which shows a colour's name with no colour beside it. A swatch there would help: "ByLayer" says nothing about which colour the object is drawn in. But the row cannot draw one honestly today. The palette's rows carry the colour as a name (COLOR_CHOICES in src/props.ts: ByLayer, ByBlock, Red and the rest) and no RGB, and the layer list's rule is that no colour is invented in the interface: the swatch paints the engine's own colorRgb. A swatch beside "ByLayer" would mean resolving the layer's colour in TypeScript. The component follows the data: when the engine's property rows carry colorRgb beside the name, build Swatch (a role="img" box named by the colour, --swatch-border, 10px) and give it the layer row and the palette row together. Until then one call site is a local rule.

  • The used mark stays local. One use, two states, no interaction, and its only rule is that

the fill carries the state where the two inks are a step apart. If a second list grows a per-row status mark, it is a component then.

Their sizes moved onto the ladder in passing (10px is --gap-10; 7px is --gap-4 plus --gap-3), with no change to what is drawn.

A row in a listbox

Decided 2026-11-11. The command palette and the assistant's slash list are role="listbox" lists driven from a text field (aria-activedescendant); each drew a Row, a <button>, inside or as its option.

  • What was wrong. Every row was a Tab stop in a list whose keyboard lives in the field, so Tab

from the palette's field walked the rows one by one. And a Row paints its own hover fill, so the row under a resting pointer and the row the arrow keys were on were both lit, in two fills.

  • The pick. Row takes option: it renders the role="option" element itself (a <div>, no

button inside it), with aria-selected from selected, aria-disabled from disabled, the id the field's aria-activedescendant names, and onPointerMove so the listbox can move its highlight under the pointer. It takes no focus and paints no hover: the one lit row is the one the listbox set.

  • Why a mode of Row, not a new component. The band is the same band: height, inset, inks and

the .14 fill. A second component would copy the recipe to change one element and two attributes. tabIndex and a hover switch as separate props were the other offer; they would leave a button inside an option, which the option role flattens for assistive tech.

  • A disabled option still takes the highlight. The palette lights a command that cannot run

and says why under the list; the option keeps the fill at the disabled ink and refuses the click.

  • A disabled current button does not (decided 2026-11-11, second pass). row.md said a

disabled selected row drops its fill and the stylesheet kept it. Both were right, each for one form. In a listbox the fill is the cursor: the keys are on that option whether or not it can run, and a list with no fill has lost its place. A button row's fill says "this is the current one, and you can act on it"; blocked, it reads as an active item that ignores the press. So .ui-row:disabled[aria-current="true"] is transparent at the disabled ink, aria-current stays for assistive tech (the row is still the current one), and .ui-row[aria-disabled="true"][aria-selected="true"] keeps --fill-active. src/ui/recipe.test.ts holds both.

A value in a dense row

Decided 2026-11-11 (the audit's open gate on the properties palette's typed values). The palette drew its own <input class="prop-input"> because Field was only the 24px form control. Field now carries all of it, in Select's vocabulary, so a typed value and a picked value in the same column are one recipe:

  • variant="inline": no stroke and no fill until the pointer or the keyboard is on it, then the

field (--border-soft, --control). Focus, a refused value and disabled win over the hover.

  • size="sm": the 20px box of a 22px row on the row's 4px inset, 24px under a coarse pointer, with

the hairline of bottom padding that puts a typed value on the label's baseline.

  • align="end": the value ends on the far edge, with lining tabular figures.
  • mixed: the "*VARIES*" stand-in in the quiet ink.
  • invalid: aria-invalid="true" and the error stroke, as before.
  • onKeyDown, onBlur, ref: commit on Enter and on leaving, restore on Escape, from the caller.
  • A value the box cuts short ends in an ellipsis and shows in full in the hint, with no

data-hint bookkeeping in the caller.

  • selectOnFocus is new behaviour, not a carry-over: a property editor wants typing to replace

the value. Leave it out for a like-for-like move.

Two values differ from the hand-drawn input, both to match the inline Select beside it: the corner is --radius-control (2px, was --radius-small, 3px) and the hover stroke is --border-soft (was --border).

The replacement, in src/components/PropertiesPanel.tsx (the text / number match):

<span class="prop-choice">
  <Field
    variant="inline"
    size="sm"
    align="end"
    ariaLabel={props.row().label}
    value={draft()}
    mixed={draft() === VARIES}
    invalid={invalid()}
    inputMode={mode() === "number" ? "decimal" : undefined}
    spellcheck={false}
    autocomplete="off"
    selectOnFocus
    onInput={(value) => {
      setDirty(true);
      setInvalid(false);
      setDraft(value);
    }}
    onKeyDown={onKeyDown}
    onBlur={() => commitText(true)}
  />
</span>

The wrapper is the one the palette's Select already sits in (a one-column grid with the overhang to the column's edge: the field stretches to it). What can then be deleted: every .prop-input rule in src/interaction.css (the base rule, its hover, :focus-visible, [aria-invalid="true"] and .is-varies), hintWhenClipped and cuts in the panel if nothing else uses them, and the .prop-input line of src/ui/recipe.test.ts, which already passes with or without the rule.

Controls that hold a value

Decided 2026-11-11, with Select, Checkbox and TextArea.

  • Native underneath, always. Each is the platform's own control with the layer's face. The

desktop app runs in three system webviews and on phones through the web build; a hand-built listbox or tick would have to re-earn type-ahead, the phone's picker, form participation and input-method handling in each.

  • Select draws its value in a span. A <select> styled directly clips without an ellipsis in

one engine, ignores text-align-last in another and takes its open list's colours from the closed control in a third. The native control lies under the face at no opacity and takes every press; the face is aria-hidden. The select stays in the flow, so the box is as wide as its longest choice asks and does not move as the value changes.

  • The mixed placeholder is not a choice. It is a hidden, disabled first option that only

exists while mixed, so it can be shown and can never be picked.

  • The checkbox's edge is the glyph ink. A hairline stroke (--border, --border-soft) is

drawn to separate surfaces that also differ in fill; an empty box differs from its surface by its edge alone, which needs 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11). --icon holds 5.23 at the least.

  • The checkbox's ring stands off the box by a hairline: at the layer's usual offset of -1 it

would be the accent ring on the accent fill.

  • One line of a TextArea is a Field's height (a 16px line, the field's padding less the

hairline: 24px), so the two can share a row.

  • A bare TextArea draws no ring. It is the only control in the layer without one, and only

because its card shows the focus; src/ui/recipe.test.ts holds ui.css to that one exception.

  • 16px under a finger. Under pointer: coarse the field, the text area and the select's

native control take font-size: max(16px, 1em), the size below which a phone zooms the page into the control. Field joined them on 2026-11-11 (it was left open here until its one form was looked at). It keeps its 24px box: under a coarse pointer it gives up its 4px of block padding, and the 16px value sits centred in the box. Looked at on the assistant's setup sheet at 390 wide with the coarse rules applied: the three fields keep their width, height and position (24px each, the same tops), nothing below them moves, and the only change is the typed value and the placeholder at 16px (.design-system/review/wE8-setup-390-coarse-*.png).

  • Section labels are not tracked. typography.md asked for 0.05em to 0.06em on uppercase

section labels; the measured header (research §2: 11px, weight 700, capitals) has none and the layer never drew any. The page moved, as it did for the hover easing.
